data.title: First Citizens is open to buying more branches post-BMO deal
data.description:
• Key insight: First Citizens' acquisition of 138 BMO branches, which closed in the third quarter, contributed to growth in both loans and deposits.
  • Expert quote: "I do think that the BMO transaction indicates that M&A will remain an important part of our growth strategy and a way for us to continue delivering value to our shareholders." — First Citizens Chief Financial Officer Craig Nix

First Citizens BancShares executives on Friday touted the successful integration of 138 branches the company acquired from BMO Financial Group, and signaled openness to similar deals in the future.

Chief Financial Officer Craig Nix said during the bank's third-quarter earnings call that while First Citizens is not pursuing whole-bank acquisitions, it remains interested in purchasing branches.

"I do think that the BMO transaction indicates that M&A will remain an important part of our growth strategy and a way for us to continue delivering value to our shareholders," Nix said. "We would look for opportunities in the space, especially opportunities to increase and improve our liquidity profile."

The BMO acquisition, which closed in the third quarter, expanded First Citizens' balance sheet and national footprint.

Raleigh, North Carolina-based First Citizens has more than 500 branches in 23 states, mostly in the Southeast and California, where it built its presence by acquiring the remains of the failed Silicon Valley Bank. The former BMO branches are primarily located in the Midwest and Great Plains.

The acquisition's full financial impact, including its benefits and costs, will be reflected in First Citizens' fourth-quarter results, executives said Friday.

The $241-billion asset bank also provided an update on its efforts to repay debt tied to its acquisition of SVB assets in March 2023. First Citizens paid $8 billion to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. in the third quarter of 2026 and an additional $1.5 billion in October, executives said.

The bank has now repaid $17 billion, or 47%, of the debt associated with the SVB acquisition and aims to eliminate the remaining balance by the end of 2027.

To finance the deal, First Citizens, the parent company of First Citizens Bank, issued a five-year, $35 billion purchase money note to the FDIC, which carries a 3.5% interest rate. The company made its first payment of $2.5 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025, primarily using proceeds from securities sales.

During the third quarter, First Citizens reported net income of $606 million, up 6.7% from a year prior. Net interest income was $1.70 billion, down 2% from a year prior.

Interest income on loans and leases totaled $2.34 billion, up slightly from $2.30 billion a year earlier and $88 million from the second quarter. The company's net interest margin was 3.07%, down from 3.26% a year earlier.

Deposits totaled $185.3 billion, up 13.5% from the same period in 2025, including $4.9 billion of deposits acquired from BMO.

Loans and leases totaled $157 billion at quarter-end, up from $145 billion a year earlier. Loans in the general bank segment grew by $633 million from the second quarter, largely driven by the BMO branch acquisition.

First Citizens' provision for credit losses fell to $55 million in the third quarter, down from $191 million a year earlier, helping offset the decline in net interest income and higher noninterest expenses.

Noninterest expenses totaled $1.57 billion in the third quarter, up from $1.49 billion a year earlier. Expenses rose $22 million from the previous quarter, driven by investments in digital infrastructure and data center modernization, executives said.

First Citizens expects expense growth to remain in the low- to mid-single digits over the medium term as the company seeks efficiencies.

"As we look at continuing to optimize and combine platforms, processes and teams, quite candidly, I think that puts downward pressure on it," Nix said.

First Citizens raised portions of its 2026 guidance. It is now projecting year-end loan balances of $158 billion to $161 billion, up around 3% from the previous guidance, driven by expansion in its commercial and general banking segments.

The bank also returned $600 million to shareholders through share repurchases during the third quarter. Its board approved a new plan authorizing the repurchase of up to $1.2 billion of Class A common shares through 2027.

data.title: Licensing process is key to yield in OCC stablecoin rule
data.description:
• Key insight: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency will assess stablecoin rewards programs on a case-by-case basis, leaving uncertainty over which arrangements comply with the GENIUS Act's ban on interest payments.
  • Forward look: If the OCC rejects an issuer's rewards program, it could spur litigation, and a future administration could take a different view of which arrangements violate the law, making even approved arrangements potentially less durable.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's final stablecoin rule leaves significant uncertainty around the extent to which issuers and their affiliates can pay customers returns on their assets without violating the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest.

In a final rule issued Wednesday, the agency removed a rebuttable presumption against stablecoin yield initially included in the proposed rule issued in March. 

Pursuant to the law, OCC's regulation maintains a narrow ban on direct yield payments from issuers to customers. OCC says it will evaluate alternative yield arrangements on an individual basis and declined to include a list of possible legal arrangements. At the same time, banks have opposed the ambiguous status quo as allowing workarounds to the ban. Issuers will need to get additional clarity from the agency, says Roman Goldstein, a partner at the Klaros Group, a fintech consultancy. 

"The OCC basically punted the yield question to the licensing and supervisory process," Goldstein said, adding that the agency rebuffed industry requests, voiced in public comments to the proposal, to provide explicit legal safe harbors. "If you're an issuer, you're going to present your program to the OCC as part of your application to issue stablecoins, and if the OCC doesn't like what it sees, it's going to tell you.

"If you don't revise your program, the OCC might deny you a license to issue stablecoins altogether," he continued. 

The final rule comes amid an ongoing debate between banks and the crypto industry over what the GENIUS Act's prohibition on yield actually means. The law explicitly bans interest payments "solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention" of stablecoins. Stever Gannon, a partner at Davis Wright Tremaine, says certain arrangements — like rewards arrangements used by credit card issuers — could wind up passing muster.

"We won't know until the applications actually get processed, but I think what we can say is some pretty plain activity-based uses of stablecoins that wind up paying yields [like] merchant discounts may be permissible," Gannon said. "Other things that should be permissible and I have a fairly high degree of confidence in this, is depositing of stablecoin pairs into liquidity pools … or depositing them into crypto lending protocols.

"Those are clearly activities that the stablecoins are put to work," he continued. "They're not obviously being held idly and they should pass muster pretty easily."

What's less clear, Gannon said, is what constitutes an indirect payment tied to productive activity of a stablecoin, and whether that definition is wide enough to create a loophole for rewards on idle stablecoins.

Gannon says he understands the agency's move to remove the presumption against yield arrangements, given there are so many possible ways to structure a rewards program. He says they have ample enforcement tools — including civil money penalties, prohibitions and prompt corrective actions — to ensure issuers stay within the boundaries they set for the stablecoin space. 

Banking trade groups like the American Bankers Association, on the other hand, have sharply criticized the decision to drop the proposed rule's presumption against yield arrangements, saying the resulting wiggle room will likely be filled by yield workarounds Congress didn't want when it wrote the law. 

"The final rule removes the OCC's originally proposed safeguards that would have addressed indirect arrangements involving affiliates, exchanges and other distribution partners," ABA President Rob Nichols said in a statement this week. "As a result, payment stablecoin issuers can provide economically equivalent yield while technically avoiding the statutory prohibition. The OCC also declined to adopt a broader presumption against arrangements designed to circumvent the ban.

"While we appreciate the OCC's recognition that additional supervisory experience may inform future action in this area, attempting to address deposit flight and economic harm after it has occurred is the wrong approach," Nichols continued. 

Advocates for small banks, including the Independent Community Bankers of America, have expressed concern about how payments stablecoins can eat into community bank lending, with financial stability effects. 

Whether stablecoins draw deposits will likely depend on the breadth and depth of customer adoption. Experts have argued that even with enticing rewards, it's not clear stablecoins will ever represent a meaningful challenge to deposits in the near term. 

Gannon argued that deposit fears could be overstated, pointing to recent FDIC data that shows community banks' deposit bases have grown in recent years, just as stablecoins have been on the rise. 

"You can debate the data eight different ways from Sunday, but those data points, which are neutral, seem to say so far community banks are doing okay," he argued. "But things could turn around." 

In the near term, litigation seems likely, says Jaret Seiberg, a financial services analyst at TD Cowen. 

"We view this rule as negative for banks as it does not fully shut down the ability of platforms to pay yield on stablecoins," he wrote in a note this week. "It reinforces our view that the Supreme Court will need to decide if the payment of rewards or yield by platforms on stable coins violates the GENIUS Act."

The legal battle could spawn if the agency takes an enforcement action against an issuer in the licensing process, says Seiberg. 

"We expect the OCC will take an enforcement action against some yield arrangement once it starts approving payment stable coin issuers," he wrote. "That issuer will then challenge the enforcement action, which will shift this fight to the court."

Goldstein says a lawsuit would require "final action" by the agency, rather than an absence of enforcement. An issuer whose application is denied for its rewards program could have standing — or a future administration could also change course.

"You can never rely on non enforcement," he said. "The OCC decides to not enforce the statute today, then the later administration can take a different position…you might be in a case where you're litigating against the future administration over what the yield prohibition means."

Issuers would be best served if they can work with the agency to get approval for their program, which could strengthen their defense against a future legal challenge if the White House changes parties. 

"The best thing issuers can do is get the OCC to approve the program they want to offer," Goldstein said. "That way, a future administration can come in and challenge it. But issuers have a pretty good defense: the agency let me do this for two years, three years."

data.title: Banks dodge early damage from PHP2Shell flaws
data.description:
• Key insight: Attackers have fired millions of attempts at the PHP2Shell flaws, but no U.S. bank or credit union has publicly reported a compromise.
  • Expert quote: "You own the risk even when a vendor runs the system," wrote Samantha Van den Broek of Crimson Oak Strategies, a compliance consultancy for credit unions.

Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review.

Attackers have fired millions of attempts to exploit two critical flaws, nicknamed PHP2Shell, in the code behind most of the world's websites this week. Federal agencies have told organizations to patch or pull vulnerable systems offline.

For U.S. banks and credit unions, the damage so far has been limited.

MSU Federal Credit Union, or MSUFCU, an $8.9 billion credit union in East Lansing, Michigan, took its website and digital banking offline Wednesday after the federal warnings.

The systems it took down ran PHP and were vulnerable to the flaws, Allison Horn, the credit union's chief of staff, told American Banker.

MSUFCU patched the systems and restored online and mobile banking Thursday. "There is no impact to member information at this time," Horn said.

No U.S. bank or credit union has yet publicly reported a compromise stemming from the PHP flaws.

Eight percent of financial services organizations that cybersecurity company Check Point tracks had an exploit attempt against them, according to a Thursday blog post from the company. Compare that to 10% across all sectors.

Check Point counts organizations that saw exploit attempts; the company said it has no way of knowing whether the attacks succeeded.

The recently disclosed vulnerabilities matter to banks because they affect PHP, a programming language that runs almost 70% of websites, according to data from web survey firm W3Techs.

At banks and credit unions, PHP can run public websites, online banking and online applications for loans and memberships.

Hosting companies or web developers run most credit unions' websites, according to a Thursday blog post from Crimson Oak Strategies, a compliance consultancy for credit unions.

Sometimes institutions build their own. MSUFCU's affected systems were "developed by and maintained by MSUFCU, not a vendor," Horn said.

What PHP2Shell is

The two flaws, tracked in the public catalog of software vulnerabilities as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each carry a severity rating of 9.2 out of 10.

Under the right conditions, they let an attacker run code on a server without logging in, according to the PHP project's Wednesday security advisory.

The flaws are in PHP itself (in how it cleans up memory after an error), so updating WordPress (a popular website platform built on PHP) or a website plugin does not fix them, according to a Wednesday blog post from Cloudflare. Administrators have to update PHP itself.

PHP released fixes in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Versions 8.1 and older get no new release from the PHP project.

Wiz, OpenAI and a security research firm named Calif found the flaws with help from artificial intelligence tools, according to blog posts from the three companies.

Lots of attacks, little proof of damage

Word of the flaws began circulating online Tuesday, a day before PHP released its fixes, according to a Wednesday post from the nonprofit PHP Foundation.

In the 10 hours before the flaws were formally announced, Cloudflare's network saw thousands of attempts to exploit them, "and millions now," Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said in a post on X late Wednesday.

Attempts are not break-ins. CISA said in a Wednesday alert that it had "not observed exploitation" of the flaws as of the alert's publication.

"The public exploits do not work against a default PHP installation," e-commerce security firm Sansec said in a Thursday update to its research post. An attack "needs specific knowledge of the target server and specific conditions on it," the update said.

There might be exceptions. VulnCheck, which sells exploit intelligence, said in a blog post that it built a working exploit that defeats a standard memory protection on servers running some versions of PHP 8.4 with PHP's recommended production settings.

While Sansec's claims suggest that the exploits are inert against many unpatched websites and web applications, VulnCheck's claims suggest that some are vulnerable.

Regardless, there are steps a financial institution can take to minimize the risk these PHP flaws pose to data security.

What banks are being told to do

The ultimate fix for the vulnerabilities is to install a patched version of PHP on every server that runs an institution's websites.

For organizations that cannot patch right away, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the National Security Agency and the FBI each urged them to take PHP systems offline in the meantime.

Following that advice has a cost. MSUFCU members went about 24 hours without online or mobile banking, though branches, the call center, ATMs and cards kept working, according to a statement from CEO April Clobes that the credit union provided to American Banker.

Statement viewing, web-based check deposit and the credit union's virtual assistant were still coming back Friday, and MSUFCU expected them to be restored by the end of the day, chief of staff Horn said.

The precautions "were necessary to ensure we could safely restore services and maintain the trust our members place in us every day," Clobes said.

In Japan, megabanks and several regional banks suspended some online services as a precaution, Jiji Press reported. The Japanese Bankers Association confirmed that the network that settles payments among nearly all of Japan's banks had not been affected, Jiji reported.

The New York Department of Financial Services, which oversees state-chartered banks, insurers and other financial companies in the state, told the firms it regulates to patch immediately and to take systems they cannot patch offline, according to an industry letter issued Thursday.

Web application firewalls, which filter malicious traffic before it reaches a website, "may provide limited protection" but "should not be used as a substitute for patching or isolation," the letter said.

For institutions that rely on vendors to run their websites, the fix runs through them. The New York regulator told firms to "coordinate with third-party service providers to assess exposure" and to confirm that those providers have fixed the flaws.

"You own the risk even when a vendor runs the system," Samantha Van den Broek wrote in the Crimson Oak post.

data.title: American Express touts AI, plans 5% downsizing
data.description:
• Key insight: Amex plans a 5% downsizing, citing a need for speed in decision-making.
  • Expert quote: "I asked the senior leadership team to streamline organization and reduce layers to speed decision making."—Amex Chairman and CEO Steve Squeri. 

American Express' plans to grow its business also includes a lower headcount.
"To accelerate innovation and win we need to become a more agile and efficient organization," Chairman and CEO Steve Squeri said during Friday's earnings call. 

Amex is reducing 5% of its jobs globally, which would be about 3,900 based on the company's 76,800 workers, a move that resulted in a $336 million charge. The company did not directly attribute the move to artificial intelligence or other technology.

"I asked the senior leadership team to streamline organization and reduce layers to speed decision making," Squeri said. 

Amex's earnings

For the quarter ending September 30, Amex reported earnings of $4.68 per share, compared to the $4.47 per share estimated by Zacks, and up from $4.14 per share during 2025's third quarter. Amex reported posted revenue of $20.06 billion, 0.34% below Zacks estimates and up from $18.43 billion the prior year.

Net income for the quarter was $3.7 billion, compared with net income of $2.9 billion a year ago. For 2026, Amex projects EPS of $17.60-$17.90, compared with its prior guidance of $17.30-$17.90 and the average analyst estimate of $17.69. It also projects $79.5 billion, in line with estimates of $79.5 billion.

"Billing and new customer growth remain healthy, but showed modest deceleration," analysts at Jeffries said in a note on Amex.

Squeri also addressed Amex's recent money-laundering related penalty.  The Federal Reserve and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency in October ordered American Express to overhaul its anti-money-laundering practices and fined Amex $350 million.

Regulators spotted $13 billion in illicit activity at the firm, including transactions with ties to insiders. The fine does not impact Amex's guidance for 2026 or outlook for 2027, and does not impose an asset cap, Squeri said, adding the company is "accountable" for addressing its AML issues. "We have earned trust over many years and won't take it for granted," Squeri said. 

AI boom and business banking

Like most payment companies, Amex is relying on new forms of artificial intelligence to improve internal processes, customer service and product development.

A big part of that is agentic commerce, or the use of AI to perform a wide range of functions, like shopping and checkout, with little or no human interaction. "It's still early in the game and volumes are still small, but AI is fundamentally changing how consumers [engage]," Squeri said.

Amex has deployed technology to vet agents and is developing coverage to "protect" agentic transactions by backing purchases made by AI agents. "AI agents are able to act on customers' behalf, but it doesn't change who the customer is," Squeri said.

During the quarter, Amex released several new AI-related initiatives for businesses, part of a larger push at Amex to internally deploy and externally sell automation for relatively mundane business processes that still require time and expense.

The company combined business payment cards, expense management software and an enhanced mobile app in a single product bundle. The corporate card lets businesses earn 1.5% cash back on eligible purchases, obtain physical and virtual cards for employees, and access expense management software.

The app automatically generates submission-ready expenses as purchases are made, an attempt to streamline manual expense reports for corporate travel or other purchases. The business tools are aimed at midsize and large businesses; and follow an earlier release of the American Express Business Savings Account and new incentive marketing designed for small businesses.

Amex's AI pipeline also includes a new payroll system with "AI-powered insights" scheduled for early 2027. Amex's agentic AI is developed internally, using technology developed by Hyper, an AI company Amex bought earlier this year; and Center, an expense management company Amex purchased in 2025. Terms for both deals were not disclosed.

In September, Amex launched a high-yield American Express Business Savings Account, with plans to  add ways for Graphite Business card members to redeem rewards for deposits into the Amex business checking account. Amex, which has offered a business checking account since 2021, has added a savings account with an annual percentage yield of 2.95% with no minimum balance requirement or monthly maintenance fees. Clients can make and receive transfers online or through Amex's app, using ACH, wire transfers or check deposits, at no cost. Or they can use same-day ACH for a $10 fee.

"The transaction of the future will be more than just a credential, it will have context," Squeri said.
Read more:

  • As fintechs nab bank charters, what's happening to BaaS?
  • Overheated data center knocked 23 credit unions offline
  • Chris Britt still says banking is broken, but Chime can fix it
  • Credit unions bulk up a business that banks long dominated

It has been a challenging environment for all financial institutions as investors adjust expectations for macro uncertainties, higher interest rates, competition, and in Amex's case, continued investment, according to analysts at William Blair.

"In our view, Amex holds a leadership position within the premium card market, and we believe incremental investments should support midteens EPS growth," William Blair analysts said in a note.Amex had a large presence at the Money 20/20 conference with a key focus on Amex Corporate and agentic commerce, according to Williiam Blair analysts. "Ensuring Amex's products remain top-of-wallet and that its membership benefit programs remain discoverable in an agentic world are key priorities," the analysts said.

data.title: How bank compliance leaders are engaging with regulators
data.description:
• Key insight: Banks are facing the challenge, and opportunity, to rework their compliance protocols as regulators are enacting broad changes to bank reporting requirements.
  • Expert quote: "A strong foundation will enable you to ensure that you are complying with consumer compliance no matter what the environment is." — Citi CCO Jennifer Taylor

As federal regulatory agencies are defining market structures in areas such as stablecoin regulation and enacting sweeping changes in bank regulation on multiple fronts, some bank compliance leaders are actively adjusting their risk management strategies.

"It's certainly an exciting time to be in banking, especially in risk management and compliance," U.S. Bank Chief Risk Officer Jodi Richard said during a panel at American Banker's Most Powerful Women In Banking Conference on Wednesday.

Nicole Anderson, principal for FS regulatory advisory services at PwC, cautioned that agencies facing staffing cuts will be relying more heavily on banks to do the legwork of risk management.

"Regulators are already telling us, 'We don't have enough resources to come in and do the same things we used to do. If you can't show us that you really have identified the risk, understand the risk and have identified appropriate controls or control gaps, you're next in line for the criticism.' We were starting to see that a little before the [regulatory] shift, but this is now going to magnify that. It's a really good time to start thinking about the fundamentals of your risk management."

Kara West, chief enterprise risk officer for Capital One, said that banks have a unique opportunity in the current regulatory environment to "push back" and engage with regulators in new ways.

"To be honest, it's a pretty tough time for them – I'd hate to be a regulator right now," she said. "We are working with our regulators to think about where we can bring them along on the changes we're making. We feel way more openness than what we've seen before, and we're trying to take advantage of that and build relationships."

Richard said that there are also new opportunities for banks to customize and adjust their risk management approaches.

"It is a great time to be a risk manager," she said. "It puts you back in the driver's seat to make sure that you're allocating resources to the highest-level emerging risk where you actually feel there is exposure, driving that a little bit more than following things that might be more interesting to a wide set of banks but not as applicable to you."

Read more:

  • OCC leaves room for stablecoin yield maneuvers in final rule
  • 'A team sport:' Responding to cyber threats in the age of AI
  • BlackRock's Mullin on a culture of 'maximum flexibility'
  • 'We could lose our edge': Bankers on competing for digital assets

Even as compliance departments are re-prioritizing their risk focuses and incorporating new tools, such as AI, Citi Chief Compliance Officer for Banking and International Jennifer Taylor said that sticking to the fundamentals of risk management will help institutions. 

"A strong foundation will enable you to ensure that you are complying with consumer compliance no matter what the environment is," she said. "This more targeted focus of risk enables us to be a bit more forward-looking and to watch out for emerging risks, which is an important way to manage risk for this fast-moving environment."

Taylor noted that much of her bank's risk management had previously revolved around risks that had happened before, but she is working to challenge some of those assumptions.

"Some of the compliance reporting metrics were created because of the situation before and that metric continued to appear in compliance reporting for years after the metric wasn't delivering any value," she said. "Now, we constantly challenge ourselves on, 'What's the purpose?' Maturing will help us continue to manage risk appropriately from a safety and soundness perspective, no matter where we manage it."

data.title: Independents lag on AI. Here's how they can catch up
data.description:
• Key insight: In the employee advisors vs. independent advisors and AI race, employee advisors remain the winners, but as structural efforts improve, independent advisors can gain ground.
  • What's at stake: proper access to the right tools means independent advisors can enjoy the same benefits as their larger counterparts.
  • Forward look: Independents doubled their use of AI in a year according to JD Power

Financial advisors who use AI have reported being more satisfied in their jobs, but the happiness is not spread evenly. Nearly three-quarters of employee advisors [employed by large firms] actively use AI, but only 42% of independent advisors do the same.

While in theory the tools are available to everyone, larger firms are better equipped to roll out AI to employees, meaning that smaller and independent firms need to accelerate their governance procedures, vetting processes and training to catch up.

The AI gap between large and small wealth firms

The gap isn't due to a lack of access to technology across the industry. Smaller firms are taking big steps, according to the JD Power study that measured advisor satisfaction and AI usage. The number of independent advisors who reported using AI jumped from 19% to 42 % in just one year, according to that study.

Rather, it all comes down to structure.

Wirehouses "have the ability to really build out this technology, integrate it into their platform, establish the rules and train the advisors," said Joe McQuaid, COO of Tampa, Florida-based Concurrent Investment Advisors, in an interview. 

James Spinelli, founder and CEO of Great Valley Advisor Group in Berwyn, Pennsylvania, grew his firm from a couple of advisors over 12 years ago to a 215-advisor firm that now manages just under $15 billion. He also developed a compensation tool called Advisor BB (Advisor Book of Business) that he deployed to about 80 RIAs before selling this past year to Bozeman, Montana-based AdvicePay. 

In the case of RIAs versus wirehouses, it is a matter of dollars and cents, he said. Bigger firms also have "the governance and they've got everything in place for that tool that they want to roll out," he said. 

For firms that want an overhaul, Spinelli believes deployment has to be strategic. 

"If I rolled out a CRM and was like 'everybody has to use Wealthbox, there's no Salesforce [or] Redtail,'" he said, adoption would rise faster, "but that's not necessarily a good thing because you take away choice [and] flexibility."

Addressing the cost and integration factors

One challenge smaller firms grapple with around AI is cost. Basic systems that meet the criteria advisors need, including proper safekeeping of client information, can run into the thousands of dollars per month. 

Dan Eyre is COO of the software company DeepVest, which recently launched Day One. Day One is the company's answer to the financial dilemma that offers smaller firms a suite of its AI tools and solutions for a low-entry price point for the first year. 

"If they have the time and the tools, they're able to better serve a client than a larger firm, where they don't get quite as much mind share from the advisor or the wealth team," he said. 

By targeting smaller firms, Eyre said, the services are a win-win for both DeepVest and its clients. 

"We know they're going to win that business," Eyre said. "They're going to use those tools and put them to better use because they don't have all the red tape."

One potential pitfall firms face without a streamlined system, according to McQuaid, is integration. Firms might not want to invest in an entire suite and opt to instead take what is known as the "bolt-on" route. When firms choose to bolt-on by adding AI features to their existing legacy software, the integration problem surfaces. 

"If AI is added to every one of the tools that we use, it still doesn't solve the problem," said McQuaid. "In the independent world… one of the issues with using all of this different fintech is [it] doesn't integrate well. The data doesn't flow back and forth between one system and another system."

For instance, an advisor using a financial planning tool and CRM that are not fully integrated with one another requires duplicate data. "If you have an integrated layer that's on top of your system that's utilizing AI, I think the experience is going to be far superior," said McQuaid.

Governance as the unlock

As governance catches up, Spinelli expects AI adoption will "skyrocket," with independents eventually surpassing their larger firm counterparts. Firms without clear governance policies risk having their advisors "skating on this fine line," he said, "of, 'oh, can I put a client's name in here? And is that going to be an issue with this tool that we're using?'"

Getting ahead on policies includes clarity around what governance should cover. 

"I think governance is extremely critical, and making sure that you have governance in place," said McQuaid, adding that governance can outline which AI tools firms use and the data they allow those tools to employ. 

"If you're not using an enterprise model, I would never put personal identifiable information (PII) in any AI model," he said. "Those governance rules are important." 

Larger firms, McQuaid said, can fold strong governance and compliance policies directly into operations. 

"Independent firms, I believe, have a lot of work that needs to be done ahead of time," he said.

Other governance measures could include:

  • Running AI tools through vendor due diligence, similarly to the process used with CRM or planning tools.
  • Asking the vendor if it trains its models on the firm's data.
  • Checking the vendor's history with client data, including around breaches or data leaks.
  • Limiting data exposure with new vendors that lack a track record rather than ruling them out.

For firms that don't have it in their budget to deploy an entire AI infrastructure from scratch, McQuaid suggests buying off-the-shelf tools as a more realistic approach. 

"The barrier of entry into building out an AI infrastructure is not low," he said. "It's a high barrier."

That barrier is why he believes more firms will move toward what he referred to as "consumption versus moving towards creation."

Another way to thoughtfully choose tools to deploy comes courtesy of firmwide pain points. A simple review of where the issues lie can result in a better understanding of the collective issues an AI tool could solve. 

"Build a plan around solving that pain," said McQuaid. "Then you can choose the tool that fits your platform."

Once tools are in place, McQuaid suggests tracking and measuring results. 

"What I found with a lot of smaller independent advisors is they're actually spending more time on the technology. So instead of it actually doing what it's supposed to do … they're spending less time with their clients and more time on the AI."

data.title: BankThink Stablecoins are essential to the health of the federal balance sheet
data.description:
• Key insight: Stablecoin issuers back their dollar-pegged assets with short-dated U.S. Treasuries. As the industry expands, they are picking up the slack left by traditional buyers who have soured on U.S. government debt.
  • Supporting data: Data from the Fed's research shows stablecoin issuers hold roughly $200 billion in U.S. Treasuries, with Tether accounting for $141 billion of the figure.

A declining global appetite for U.S. Treasuries has been in the spotlight, with Japan, China and France leading the pack as sellers. Analysts cite inflation concerns, Trump tariffs, lack of fiscal restraint, and an escalating global bond sell-off as factors behind the pivot away from Treasuries, but data also suggests private investors and stablecoin issuers have emerged as new sources of demand, and may play a role in bolstering the U.S. dollar.

According to the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, rising stablecoin issuer demand for short-dated Treasuries is reducing the impact of foreign governments selling U.S. Treasuries.

Data from the Fed's research shows stablecoin issuers hold roughly $200 billion in U.S. Treasuries, with Tether (USDT issuer) accounting for $141 billion of the figure. This puts Tether ahead of several U.S. allies who were traditionally large buyers.

The Fed further estimates that if the current demand trend sustains alongside stablecoin market cap expansion, stablecoin issuers' ownership of short-duration U.S. Treasuries could reach $400 billion by 2030. Standard Chartered, meanwhile, projects the stablecoin market capitalization to surpass $2 trillion by 2028; if it hits that milestone, short-dated Treasury bill demand could rise to $1 trillion. This level of increasing and consistent demand for U.S. Treasuries provides a stabilizing force, protecting USD's status as the world's reserve currency, and, therefore, U.S. interest rates and related markets like real estate. With more than $30 trillion in debt, the U.S. borrows $10 billion net every business day. It's not ideal from a geopolitics standpoint to be reliant on global powers like China to continue to purchase U.S. debt. The increased purchasing power of stablecoin issues helps to even-out that power dynamic. 

Demand for stablecoins and the resulting impact on Treasury markets has been driven by financial institutions and financial technology companies pushing to tokenize assets by bringing them on-chain. Self-published data from Visa highlighted exponential growth in its stablecoin card programs, with more than 160 active worldwide and payment volume up 200% year over year. Circle's Payments Network currently has 175 financial institutions enrolled, and the recently launched Arc Level 1 live blockchain network includes the Intercontinental Exchange, Mastercard, Visa, Standard Chartered, and BlackRock among its validator members. 

These figures highlight the critical role stablecoins play in transfers, foreign exchange, payments, and lending, including real-world asset tokenization where stocks, commodities, Treasuries, and more are being brought on-chain for 24/7 trading in crypto markets and soon on Wall Street. 

Due to their forays into tokenized assets, fintech and TradFi companies are accelerating stablecoin adoption and contributing to their growing impact on the U.S. economy. 

Read more:

  • OCC leaves room for stablecoin yield maneuvers in final rule
  • 'We could lose our edge': Bankers on competing for digital assets
  • Fintechs asking for, and receiving, bank charters in 2026
  • Inside Fifth Third's 'innovation economy' ambitions

Treasury demand is central to the stablecoin flywheel because on-chain settlement requires a dollar that essentially "lives" online, and each dollar minted by a regulated issuer is backed by a short-dated Treasury or repo position.
The recently passed GENIUS Act also requires that issuers back every token 1:1 and limits reserves to cash, deposits or Treasuries dated less than 93 days. 

With the total stablecoin market cap sitting at $305 billion and the two largest issuers (Tether (USDT) and Circle (USDC) holding approximately $220 billion in Treasury-linked reserves, this figure, and its impact on U.S. Treasury markets, is expected to grow as stablecoin volumes expand with institutional finance initiatives related to asset tokenization.

The trajectory of the circulating supply of tokenized equities has skyrocketed since the Sept. 15 failed procedural cloture vote for the CLARITY Act in the U.S. Senate. After the failed vote, the CFTC and SEC stepped in, announcing several rules that let stablecoin and RWA issuers get busy. The writing is no longer "on the wall." The mass adoption and integration of stablecoins to the U.S. and global economy is happening as we speak. 

The accelerating pace at which tokenized assets are being brought on-chain, and stablecoins' role in these processes, validate the view that stablecoins are essential to the growth of the U.S. economy and future of capital formation across global markets.

data.title: How scrutiny of private-credit valuations will impact banks
data.description:
• Key insight: The SEC and state insurance regulators are trying to ensure that the valuations of opaque, illiquid private-credit loans are accurate. Changes in how those investments are valued could have knock-on effects for banks. 
  • What's at stake: The links between private credit, life-insurance companies and banks could contribute to systemic instability, experts warn.

Private-credit valuations are coming under increased scrutiny from federal and state regulators, setting off alarm bells about banks' growing exposure to hard-to-value, illiquid private assets.

Private-credit assets typically are illiquid, individually negotiated loans that don't trade on any secondary market. Because the assets cannot be priced, they have historically been offered only to accredited investors. 

But Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Paul Atkins is seeking to expand access to individual investors. Last month, the SEC put asset managers on notice to "maintain vigor" around valuations. The reminder came on the heels of explosive growth in private credit.  Specifically within registered funds, private credit surged to $270 billion in 2025, a 60% jump from $170 billion in 2020, the SEC said.

"The growing accessibility of private assets, including private credit, calls for a critical reminder that registrants maintain rigor over how these assets are valued and how those valuations and asset risk characteristics are disclosed to investors," SEC Chief Accountant Kurt Hohl wrote in a joint statement with Brian Daly, director of the SEC's division of investment management. 

Some of the banking industry's exposure to private credit is through life insurers. Life insurers an estimated $1 trillion invested in private credit, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners, a trade group representing state regulators, pegged insurers' exposure at $1.21 trillion as of the end of 2025. Banks have significant counterparty exposure to life insurers.

Life-insurance companies are among the major firms financing the AI data center buildout, with significant exposure to AI-linked debt. If AI-linked loans default or lose value, losses could spread through the financial system, increasing the risk of contagion to banks, some experts warn. 

Historically, life insurers have relied on safe assets like Treasuries and high-grade corporate bonds to meet future policyholder obligations. But private-equity firms have taken over numerous life insurers, and they sought higher returns in low interest-rate environments by investing heavily in private credit and loans to affiliated companies. 

What's more, banks' ties to the private-credit market could deepen as a result of several proposed changes to bank capital rules. Lower risk weights could make it more attractive for banks to finance or hold certain private credit-related assets.

The shift toward illiquid, but potentially higher-yielding private loans has sparked ramped-up scrutiny. 

"It's important to understand how important valuation is to the SEC," said John Mahon, a partner at the law firm Cleary Gottlieb. "Investors have to have confidence in the valuation process because you need robust valuation in order to get comfortable with the expansion of retail products." 

Nadja Dreff, senior vice president and sector lead for global insurance and pension ratings at Morningstar DBRS, said not every insurer is suited to holding illiquid, opaque investments. 

"We haven't gone through a full credit cycle so we don't know how these investments will perform," Dreff said. "The complexity also varies. There are structures that are quite complex and not easily understood." 

Importantly, the SEC's statement is part of a proposal that would allow registered investment advisers to charge performance fees to a broader range of investors, mutual funds and exchange traded funds, in the push to expand individual investors' access to private markets. 

Whenever there are performance-based fees involved, Mahon said, "you have to have confidence in valuations because now the fund managers are being paid even more concretely on those valuations."

Dreff said there is a potential conflict of interest when private-equity owners receive fees from insurers they own. Morningstar DBRS analysts are assessing whether asset managers' parent companies have "undue influence," and whether insurance companies are making independent investment decisions, she said.

"There could be a mismatch in the relationship where the asset manager or private-equity owner also receives fees from the insurer that it owns," Dreff said. "The more investments that the private-equity owner could offer up and provide, that the insurer accepts as appropriate and buys into their portfolio, the higher the fees that the parent or the private-equity owner earns."

Banks' exposure to private credit

Banks' counterparty exposure to life insurers comes through credit lines, funding agreement notes, derivative contracts and syndicated private loans, experts said. If an insurer experiences a run or regulatory seizure, banks could face collateral haircuts and broader systemic instability, experts said.

Though statutory accounting rules require very high reserves for certain products like term life insurance and universal life insurance, many insurers routinely cede liabilities and transfer a portion of their risk to reinsurers, which reduces the amount of statutory reserves they are required to hold on their balance sheets.

Mayra Rodriguez Valladares, a risk consultant and managing principal at MRV Associates, said state regulators are also pushing insurance companies to be more forthcoming about their risk exposures. 

"Private-equity firms are sitting on a lot of assets that they haven't been able to sell," said Valladares, who trains bankers and regulators about risks they are exposed to. "State regulators are looking under the hood of these life-insurance companies. It's very opaque to the people to whom it should be transparent." 

Tom Gober, a forensic accounting and expert witness, claims that major insurance carriers are holding tens of billions in short-term funding agreements while carrying razor-thin cash reserves meant to cover policyholders' future payouts. He has alleged that some insurance companies have been masking their true financial health through offshore reinsurance and affiliated investments.

"Everyone is starting to talk about how this is not the insurance industry we used to know," said Gober. "It's a high-risk, dangerous, illiquid industry."

A core reason for the higher risk is that private-equity firms and asset managers have bought life insurers and increasingly have invested in affiliated businesses. Last year, there were 139 life insurers with a combined $321 billion of affiliated investment assets, according to the National Association of Insurance Commissioners.

The NAIC, which creates model laws and accounting rules, has developed several proposals aimed at getting a grasp of life insurers' valuations of private credit — in part because current reporting requirements vary substantially.

The NAIC is conducting a 2026 year-end review to address the adequacy of life-insurer reserves, also with a focus on valuations. The review seeks to connect the quality of asset valuations to the assumptions used to demonstrate that adequate reserves have been set aside for policyholders.

In 2025, life insurers' exposure to private-credit funds, privately rated bonds and business development companies totaled $544 billion, the NAIC has found. 

A key issue cited by both the SEC and the NAIC involves so-called Level 3 assets, whose fair value cannot be determined by market pricing and is based on what the industry calls "unobservable inputs." The NAIC also is considering whether operating subsidiaries and difficult-to-value private structures need different treatment.

Read more:

  • Inside Fifth Third's 'innovation economy' ambitions
  • Citi hires Google's director of engineering, shuffles AI leaders
  • Wells Fargo prevails in pay fight with former CEO Tim Sloan
  • BMO's top US executive to depart in leadership shuffle

Dreff said Morningstar DBRS analysts currently are assessing the quality of individual insurers' risk-management frameworks and overall governance.

"Once we get comfort around that, it gives us an added sort of confidence that an insurer has the appropriate structures and guardrails in place to protect policyholders," she said. 

As for the SEC, it has said the need for accurate valuations applies to all private funds. The agency has cautioned firms against using boilerplate language or ignoring current market conditions when evaluating assets.

"The whole system is stable only if insurance companies have illiquid liabilities to match their illiquid private-credit investments," said Dreff.

data.title: Looking ahead, Huntington sees growth, warnings signs
data.description:
• Key insight: Huntington remains excited about the opportunities its new markets and national lending verticals present, but CEO Steven Steinour says high levels of market turbulence are a cause for concern. 
  • Supporting data: The company projects earnings of between $1.75 to 1.83 per share in 2027.

Though some of Huntington Bancshares' business lines struggled in the third quarter, commercial-and-industrial lending hit on all cylinders.

The Columbus, Ohio-based company's C&I balances grew 3% to $94 billion during the three months ended Sept. 30, helping to offset declines in its commercial real estate, residential mortgage and auto-loan portfolios.

"The environment for commercial customers is still constructive," Brant Standridge, Huntington's president, said Thursday on a call with analysts. "We're still seeing customers pursue growth opportunities. We're still seeing customers execute on a number of strategic initiatives, and I would say [capital expenditure] is still very strong."

The C&I expansion reflects progress in the $287.8 billion-asset Huntington's strategy of adding national commercial-lending verticals, according to executives at the bank.

It's launched 14 verticals since 2015, including one hatched in August that focuses on serving community and property associations and their management partners. Earlier this month, Huntington unveiled an international corporate banking group to work with multinational companies entering or expanding in the U.S.

"That group of corporate and specialty businesses generated $11 billion of loan growth in the last year. That is still in the very early stages," Standridge told American Banker on Thursday.

Headwinds outside of C&I

Outside the C&I arena, Huntington's loan-growth efforts produced more mixed results. There were small gains in home-equity and marine and recreational vehicle lending, but balances in the CRE, home mortgage and automobile portfolios declined by a combined $872 million from June 30, 2026, levels.

The CRE issues stemmed from a surge in construction-loan paydowns in July and August. Huntington slowed auto and mortgage production on its own due to pricing concerns.

"We're seeing areas where we're just not getting risk-adjusted returns," Chairman and CEO Steve Steinour said on the conference call. "We'd rather return capital to shareholders than put it out at what we think would be very low returns, in some cases not even meeting our minimum expectations."

The third quarter was Huntington's first full three-month stretch since converting former Cadence Bancorp customers to its operating system in June. In January, it converted former Veritex Holdings clients.

Acquiring Houston-based Cadence and Dallas-based Veritex added more than $60 billion of assets and expanded Huntington's footprint in Texas and the Southeast.

Commenting on the conference call, Standridge said Huntington has had good success in retaining bankers and clients from Veritex and Cadence, and believes its prospects for growing revenue in the new markets are better than previously expected.

"We're feeling positive about where we are and very optimistic about the opportunities that these markets present for the company," Standridge said.

Huntington reported third-quarter net income totaling $680 million, roughly level with its $686 million second-quarter profit. Year-over-year comparisons were skewed by the additions of Cadence and Veritex.

The third-quarter result amounted to $0.33 per share. Excluding merger-related expenses, Huntington's adjusted earnings-per-share totaled $0.38, topping the consensus estimate of $0.35, according to S&P Capital IQ.

Huntington reported deposits totaling $224.7 billion on Sept. 30, up 1% on a quarter-over-quarter basis. Loans of $191.4 billion were also up 1%.

Read more:

  • Inside Fifth Third's 'innovation economy' ambitions
  • Citi hires Google's director of engineering, shuffles AI leaders
  • Wells Fargo prevails in pay fight with former CEO Tim Sloan
  • Bank OZK, heavy in CRE loans, makes progress in diversifying

Jefferies analyst David Chiaverini characterized Huntington's results as "mixed." In a research note, he said earnings per share were higher than expected, but he also pointed to the muted loan growth.

Huntington, which has reported earnings totaling $0.91 per share through the first nine months of 2026, is projecting earnings per share of $1.75 to $1.83 in 2027. The company believes it will achieve a return on tangible common equity of 17% to 18%, above the 14.6% reported for the quarter ended Sept. 30.

At the same time, Steinour said uncertainty surrounding the ultimate impact of tariffs, interest-rate hikes and inflation means Huntington will tread carefully.

"Having been around this for four-and-one-half decades, I'm a little more cautious, perhaps, than some of my peers," Steinour said. "There's just so much volatility in the markets today. I don't recall the amount of challenges that we're seeing globally at any time in my career. We're going to be sensitive to that in terms of how much volume we want to add."

data.title: Bread: Inflation making spending 'increasingly selective'
data.description:
• Key insights: While credit sales grew 9% in the third quarter, Bread Financial CEO Ralph Andretta said that consumers with lower credit scores showed greater selectivity in their purchasing patterns.
  • What's at stake: Persistent inflation and high gas prices are starting to change consumers' purchasing patterns, but have yet to impact overall spending or repayment rates. 

Persistent inflation and high gas prices have yet to impact consumer spending or repayment rates, according to Bread Financial, but some consumers are being more cautious. 

Bread Financial CEO Ralph Andretta said on the company's third quarter earnings call Thursday that consumer behavior continued to remain resilient, but that spending "was increasingly intentional. 

"Higher credit quality cardholders remained a consistent source of strength, while consumers with lower credit risk scores showed greater selectivity in their purchasing patterns," Andretta said. 

Bread's credit sales increased 9% year over year to $7.4 billion as consumers with higher credit scores continued to spend and consumers with lower credit scores adapted to the higher cost of fuel by shopping for deals and pulling back on some discretionary spending, such as dining out at restaurants.

"Consumers are obviously spending more on fuel, and we're seeing restaurant spending come down," Chief Financial Officer Perry Beberman told American Banker in an interview following the company's earnings call. "Fast casual, no change, but full-service restaurant spend is lower. Similarly, we're seeing lower [travel and entertainment] costs, which means customers are making choices to make sure they're still able to meet their needs within their budget." 

That doesn't mean consumers aren't traveling, Beberman said. "We actually have the same number of hotel stays, but the average transactions are down. Middle America is seeking deals on hotel stays or trading down from a higher end hotel to more value-priced hotels." 

Consumers were staying current on their bills, too. Bread's delinquency rate decreased 47 basis points year over year to 5.57%, and its net loss rate dropped 99 basis points to 6.4%. 

Looking to the fourth quarter, Beberman said he expects holiday spending to be delayed this year due to the election in November. 

"Anytime you're in a period like this where you've got an election right in the middle of it, retailers are usually hold back on their advertising and their deals because everyone's mailbox is getting filled up with political campaign ads," Beberman said. 

Still, Bread is expecting a "pretty strong" holiday shopping season, Beberman said. 

"Higher end consumers are going to spend and spend well," he said. "Middle income folks are going to continue to spend for their kids and families and friends and go out and do things. They're just going to be a little more value conscious." 

Broadly, Bread posted a "solid quarter" that sets the company up to finish off the year strong, according to Keefe Bruyette & Woods analyst Sanjay Sakhrani. "We left earnings with more conviction in the fundamentals and our estimates next year," he said. Revenue was up 5% year over year to $1 billion, while end-of-period loans increased 7% to $18.9 billion. And net interest margin came in at 18.89%, an increase of 40 basis points from the second quarter and 8 basis points from a year ago.

data.title: Visa, Mastercard bet on AI, crypto ahead of earnings
data.description:
• Key insight: Visa and Mastercard both released several AI and blockchain-related products in recent days. 
  • What's at stake: The credit card companies announce third quarter earnings next week, and investors will be looking at revenue sources such as value-added non-payment services. 

With card-issuing banks pressured to build strategies for agentic commerce and digital assets, Visa and Mastercard are expanding their abilities to sell into these trends. 

Both card brands have released services in the past few days, and in the case of Visa, there were rumors of a potential $2.5 billion deal to acquire cryptocurrency technology firm Fireblocks. Visa said it does not comment on rumors or speculation, while Fireblocks did not return a request for comment (Fireblocks denied Visa talks in crypto site Coindesk.)

Supplier payments

Even before talk of a Fireblocks acquisition, Visa recently released several tools designed for agentic commerce and digital assets. Earlier this week, the card company introduced services for corporate payments, including new analytics for supplier spending, virtual-card fraud prevention, and a live pilot enabling trusted AI agents to complete B2B invoice payments."The B2B world is filled with very routine manual processes that are just begging for automation," Darren Parslow, global head of Visa Commercial Solutions, told American Banker. 

The new analytics, called SESA 2.0, use AI to produce spend analysis and to help businesses identify high-potential supplier opportunities. Another product, Visa Commercial Fraud Solutions, helps issuers and businesses validate suppliers, authenticate virtual-card payment activity and apply controls before a payment is approved."What we're really trying to do is build the ecosystem for agentic commerce," Parslow said.

An additional initiative, a pilot with Billtrust, enables trusted AI agents to initiate and help complete approved invoice payments through supplier portals, using Visa Intelligent Commerce and Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol.

"What's great about this pilot is it addresses both sides, the buyers and suppliers, for a fully automated payment from invoice approval to supplier acceptance," Parslow said. 

On the digital asset front, Visa this week took its Visa Direct stablecoin project out of pilot testing. In the initial deployment, Inyo Global, a Visa Direct processor that has banks, fintechs and payment companies among its clients, is supporting stablecoin processing for Visa Direct clients and partners. These businesses will have the option to  prefund cross-border payouts through Visa Direct with USDC in near real time, rather than relying solely on traditional funding windows.

"The next chapter for stablecoins is adoption," said Vira Platonova, global head of Visa Direct. In a release. 

Visa's digital asset strategy could get a boost if it were to acquire Fireblocks, which sells institutional custody, stablecoin settlement and tokenization, among other services. Visa and Mastercard have both made stablecoin support a key pillar of their value-added services strategies–or their quest to draw revenue from sources beyond card payments. 

Fruit from Mastercard's BVNK deal

Mastercard's moves over the past week include launching Global Money Platform with BVNK, with Nuvei, Marqeta, Ontop and Beem among the first users. The platform enables banks, fintechs and businesses to use software or an application programming interface to support traditional currency and stablecoins. Mastercard Move supports local bank payouts, with more than 40 currencies planned to be available by 2017.

Mastercard closed a $1.8 billion deal to acquire digital asset technology firm BVNK in August, supplying Mastercard with tools to scale digital assets–a goal Visa could also address if it acquired Fireblocks. 

"Stablecoins used to be just about powering crypto trading. It's now becoming a payment instrument and a way to store value as well," Raj Dhamodharan, executive vice president of blockchain and digital asset products at Mastercard, told American Banker. 

Mastercard in recent days also launched Stablecoin Security, a product designed to assess fraud and other criminal risk before funds move from traditional rails to blockchain, and a demonstration of Agent Pay for Machines. This product enables AI agents to autonomously locate and pay for digital services based on rules set by humans. The move to agentic commerce builds on top of earlier moves the card network made to prepare for AI payments, including agentic AI protocols.

"With a lot of agentic commerce options, you can use these cards on the street today, they can be paired with a trusted agent," Dhamodharan said. 

Courting investors

Visa reports earrings on Tuesday after the market closes, while Mastercard reports Thursday before the opening. 

Mastercard's stock is up about 11% since late October 2025; while Visa's stock is up about 20%. Mastercard's most recent earnings report beat analysts' expectations, as did Visa's earnings. 

 In a research note, KeyBanc Capital Markets notes that Visa and Mastercard's work in agentic commerce positions the card networks well to offer services within guidance for agentic commerce that a group of large banks issued earlier this year. 

Read more:

  • As fintechs nab bank charters, what's happening to BaaS?
  • Overheated data center knocked 23 credit unions offline
  • Chris Britt still says banking is broken, but Chime can fix it
  • Credit unions bulk up a business that banks long dominated

"The [bank guidance] paper calls for secure and auditable methods to enter payment credentials and authorize purchase intents, and states unsafe practices should be discouraged and, where possible, prohibited naming raw card credential entry into websites, prioritizing payment methods with lower protections, and non-compliance with payment scheme rules," KeyBanc's analysts said. "In our view, an issuer consortium arguing for tokenized credentials and scheme rule enforcement supports the network trust and tokenization thesis we have outlined previously, and aligns with the direction of Visa Intelligent Commerce and Mastercard Agent Pay,".
More broadly, analysts from FT Partners said payment growth should remain strong for both Visa and Mastercard during the third quarter, overcoming any economic pressure. 

 "The [messaging] on the health of the U.S. consumer should remain upbeat. Card volume growth in the third quarter from the major issuing banks was in-line with the second quarter, with continued strength across debit and credit, implying no change in mix between discretionary and non-discretionary spend," FT Partners analysts said in a research note.

data.title: 'Tell me what you think': Challenges of managing AI users
data.description:
• Key insight: Leaders at financial firms are figuring out how to plan for armies of autonomous agents as they grapple with where, what kind and how much AI staff should be using today.
  • Expert quote: "The leadership challenge and the talent challenge that we're all going to have is, I don't want to read copilots' recommendations. The same way that if you stand in front of a board, they don't want to have you reading your notes. They want to hear your perspective and your judgment. And so I'm trying to push really hard on the teams to say, don't give me what the agents or the LLMs are telling you. Tell me what you think, and do it in a way that I know it's your thought. It can be informed by those, but I need to know it's your actual thought."—Kristin Lesher, chief wholesale banking officer at Truist.

At Franklin Templeton, more than 6,000 AI agents have been deployed that act like individual employees. They report to manager AI agents that evaluate whether they are doing their work properly or need to be reprogrammed or even turned off. The manager agents report to HR agents, which report to human beings.
"It sounds a little sci-fi-ish, but these agents are actually taking action in your organization every day," said Sandy Kaul, head of digital assets and innovation at the investment firm, at American Banker's Most Powerful Women in Banking conference this week. "The way they're operating needs to be monitored, and you need another agent to monitor that," she said.

Lisa Farkovits, managing director and head of model and AI risk management at Barclays, said that as firms start to treat AI agents like employees, "You can go to a phone book, you can query an agent the way you would a human employee and get an answer."

Kaul and Farkovits are two among many leaders in the financial industry grappling with decisions about where and how they should allow AI agents to operate autonomously within their firms, and how to monitor and govern them.

At Truist and M&T Bank , AI agents do not work independently as if they were individual employees. But both banks are creating frameworks, guardrails and governance that will make it safe to put autonomous AI agents into production.

The banks do provide agentic AI tools to employees to help them with their work.

At M&T, agentic AI is used in about 75% of work across the organization, according to Rhea Rajwani, head of AI and emerging banking solutions risk.

Truist lets staff use agentic AI for two purposes: to provide better client advice and products and services, and to enable teams to be more productive and efficient.

"It's not, 'here are these cool technologies, let's go find a place to apply them in the bank,'" said Kristin Lesher, Truist's chief wholesale banking officer. "It's, 'here's what we need to do as a business, and how can the technology help us do that better?'"

For instance, Lesher said she could set up an agent to gather information and help create client presentations.

"But only I can use that agent," she said. "It can't go do things in our company. It can only help me be more productive. The humans are delivering the information and the advice to the clients, but the agents are helping the humans be faster and more productive in the way that they do it."

One challenge of letting bankers use AI agents as virtual assistants is that everyone wants to use "the absolute best and fastest version of it that can do the work as completely as possible because that feels awesome," Lesher said. The company has been studying the costs, projecting how they may rise over time, determining where employees could have used a much cheaper method for a task, and determining which tools should be used for different capabilities.

Another issue is employees' outsourcing their critical thinking to these tools.

"The leadership challenge and the talent challenge that we're all going to have is, I don't want to read copilots' recommendations," Lesher said. "The same way that if you stand in front of a board, they don't want to have you reading your notes. They want to hear your perspective and your judgment. And so I'm trying to push really hard on the teams to say, don't give me what the agents or the LLMs are telling you. Tell me what you think, and do it in a way that I know it's your thought. It can be informed by those, but I need to know it's your actual thought."

When Truist does one day have agentic AI teammates, they will need to have permissions, goals and objectives, Lesher said. "They get a performance review, and you've got to be able to hire them, fire them, all the same things you do with humans," she said. "We're in the preparatory phases of that, but it will be a reality that all leaders will manage teams that consist of both human beings and digital teammates."

Responsibility for AI agents will be owned jointly by business leaders, risk managers and the technology team, she said. "It's business-led in terms of what what we really need as a company, risk owns making sure that we have all the right governance routines around what we're allowing agents to do or not do and what information they have access to or not, and technology owns the ability to both protect the perimeter from the outside risk that could come in, as well as the kill switch," Lesher said. Every agent Truist creates will have a kill switch that can be activated by the technology team when they see a threat emerging.

data.title: Merrill announces laser-targed advisor bonus incentives for 2027
data.description:
• Key insight: As wirehouses seek to retain and recruit advisors, Merrill becomes the latest firm to avoid rocking the boat by making only minor changes to its pay policies in 2027.
  • Supporting data: Among the tweaks, Merrill is raising the minimum strategic asset requirement to qualify for its Growth Award from $5 million to $7.5 million.
  • Expert quote:  "You know, if you're flat, nothing's really changing. It's just people on the margin, maybe, that potentially could lose out."— Andrew Tasnady, founder of Tasnady & Associates

For the second straight year, Merrill is tweaking its compensation policies to encourage advisors to bring in more client assets and offer banking products, while leaving basic compensation unchanged.

The Bank of America subsidiary announced its advisor compensation strategy for 2027 on Thursday. The changes include revisions to its Merrill Growth Award policies designed to reward advisors for bringing in new assets and client households and a new award to encourage lending to clients. At the same time, Merrill is planning no changes next year to the basic grid determining how much advisors get to take home when they generate certain amounts of revenue annually.

"We look at compensation every year to make sure it supports our long-term strategy and rewards advisors for strong performance," Merrill Chief Operating Officer Patricio Diaz said in a statement. "This year, that meant making a few targeted updates that reflect the evolving needs of our clients and the breadth of capabilities our advisors bring to them."

READ MORE: What to expect in advisor pay in 2026

With advisor pay, consistency can be best

While wealth managers often use pay policies to nudge advisors toward arranging loans for clients and similar actions, most are reluctant to make big changes from year to year. Survey results released this month by the research firm Cerulli Associates suggested that advisors looking to join new firms value pay policies that are not only generous but also consistent.

Andrew Tasnady, a compensation consultant and the founder of Tasnady & Associates, said Merrill's changes for 2027 are largely neutral. They're likely to be welcome to advisors whose business is growing but could go unnoticed by others.

"You know, if you're flat, nothing's really changing," Tasnady said. "It's just people on the margin, maybe, that potentially could lose out. But it's probably not that many people."

Merrill is the third of the so-called wirehouses to announce its pay policies for 2027. Of the two others, UBS is making no changes to its basic pay grid, while Morgan Stanley is adjusting its grid so that advisors will need to produce more revenue in order to have the same take-home pay next year. The fourth wirehouse, Wells Fargo, usually announces its compensation policies this month.

With no changes to its basic grid, Merrill will most likely maintain its place in the middle of the wirehouse pack for advisors at various revenue-production levels. Merrill advisors who generate $1 million in revenue credits a year now get to keep $465,000 — more than their peers at Morgan Stanley but less than those at Wells Fargo and UBS. At the $2 million production level, Merrill advisors keep just over $1 million, which is also less than is paid at Wells and UBS but more than at Morgan Stanley. 

READ MORE: Merrill boasts of 75% graduation rate for its advisor training program 

Merrill Growth Award changes, New Lending Growth Award

Basic advisor pay is usually augmented by awards and bonuses meant to encourage advisors to pursue certain types of business. Merrill's compensation adjustments next year are solely to these sorts of incentives.

The firm is changing some of the qualification criteria for its Merrill Growth Award. The policy pays qualifying advisors an award equal to 12 basis points (0.12%) of up to $50 million on what the firm calls "strategic flows" — such as money in managed accounts, banking deposits and lending arrangements. The payout percentage falls for flows in excess of $50 million.

Advisors qualify for the award by hitting a minimum amount of assets or a minimum number of client households; both criteria will increase next year. 

Starting in 2027, advisors will have to bring in a minimum of $7.5 million in strategic flows, up from $5 million, or obtain four new household credits, up from three. (Merrill generally provides one "credit" for each new household but may allot more for large households.)

Separately, Merrill is eliminating its current "elite award" for advisors who bring in more than $150 million in strategic flows and replacing it with three new elite awards. Those new awards will be given to advisors who either bring in $50 million or more in net inflows into managed accounts or $10 million or more into checking or savings accounts, or help arrange $10 million or more in total loans to clients. Advisors who qualify for the elite awards receive a 50% higher addition to their standard Merrill Growth Award payout.

Merrill is also introducing the New Lending Growth Award, an incentive that will pay 10 basis points (.10%) on $10 million or more in total loans arranged for clients and 20 basis points on $25 million or more in loans.

Tasnady said firms will occasionally adjust rewards to remind advisors what their priorities should be.

"A lot of times with bonuses, you have to make a tweak just to keep people's attention on them," he said. "People get used to whatever the compensation is. So it just is like a slight energy jolt just to refocus or continue to try to focus as much attention as possible on those key drivers."

READ MORE: Merrill underlines recruiting ambitions with $2.2B advisor pulled from JPMorgan 

Recent pay changes, revival in recruiting

Merrill's efforts to encourage advisors to bring in new assets and households and arrange loans have also borne fruit. Merrill Wealth Management saw its total client balances — which includes investments, deposits and loans — rise by 9% year over year in the third quarter to $4.2 trillion. Merrill also reported adding 4,200 households net with $500,000 or more investable assets, a figure up 17% year over year.

Merrill started paying its growth awards in 2024, the same year it abandoned an unpopular growth grid that offered advisors more of a mix of rewards and punitive measures for attaining or failing to attain certain goals. Since then, the firm has mostly avoided big changes to its pay policies and instead stuck to adjustments around the edges.

This year, for instance, Merrill lowered its payouts for advisors who work with "small" households — those with between $250,000 and $500,000 in assets and loans. Advisors now receive a cut equal to only 20% of the revenue credits they generate from these clients. 

Merrill and Bank of America have meanwhile recommitted to recruiting advisors. In a call discussing the firm's earnings last week, Merrill Wealth Management co-head Lindsay Hans said the firm so far this year has more than doubled assets brought in through recruited advisors.

"As we look ahead, we've got continued momentum," Hans said. "October is really shaping up to be the strongest start to the fourth quarter since we relaunched experienced advisor recruiting in 2024, and we have a number of contracts in place. At the same time, we continue to maintain strong experience advisor retention, and that reflects the access to the Bank of America and Merrill platform to be able to serve clients and again support them at every stage of their careers."

data.title: D.C.-area bank sees profits rise as new CEO seeks turnaround
data.description:
• Key insight: Eagle Bank is showing signs of progress in reducing credit risk and improving profitability, but loan and deposit balances remain below year-ago levels as the bank invests in hiring to support future growth.
  • Supporting data: Eagle's net income grew to $24.2 million in the third quarter, up from a net loss of $67.5 million a year prior.

Eagle Bancorp reported its biggest quarterly profit in three years, as new CEO Stephen Curley works to turn around a Washington, D.C,-area lender that racked up big losses last year.
The Bethesda-Maryland based bank, which has struggled with troubled office loans,

posted third-quarter net income of $24.2 million, compared with a net loss of $67.5 million a year earlier.

Eagle saw the value of its criticized and classified loans fall by $448 million, or 41%, from a year earlier. But its nonperforming assets rose 24.5% from a year earlier to $166 million, largely because it moved a $56 million Maryland affordable multifamily loan relationship into nonperforming status. 

Curley, who was hired in May after previously working at Western Alliance Bancorp, said Thursday that the increase was partly driven by the bank's decision to address the maturing loan. Despite the rise in nonperforming assets, he said, the bank is making progress.
