"When I step back from the individual metrics, I see a company well positioned with less credit risk, a strong capital base and a renewed capacity to grow," Curley said on the bank's earnings call. "Our job now is to convert that progress into stronger returns for our shareholders."

While continuing to address the bank's balance sheet remains a priority, Curley said he is also focused on hiring to support growth in deposits and loans. The bank announced the appointment of Corey Muñoz as chief people officer, a role that includes overseeing employee retention and recruitment.

"One of my priorities since arriving has been making sure we have the leadership and talent to execute against the opportunities we see across Eagle," Curley said. "We've also added experienced bankers tasked with bringing in new business and growing deposits and loans."

The nearly $10 billion-asset bank has increased hiring in Baltimore following its September announcement that it would expand its commercial banking business there, Curley said.

The hiring push has contributed to higher expenses. Noninterest expenses rose to $47.1 million from $41.9 million in the same period a year earlier, driven primarily by a $7 million increase in salaries and employee benefits.

"We're beginning to see the activity we expected from those investments, and expect that momentum to continue through the fourth quarter and well into 2027," Curley said.

But the bank's investments in future growth have yet to translate into higher loan and deposit balances.

Total loans, including loans held for sale, stood at $6.6 billion at the end of the third quarter, down from $7.3 billion a year earlier, largely because of a decline in income-producing real estate loans. Total deposits fell to $8 billion from $9.46 billion on Sept. 30, 2025.

The bank's provision for credit losses was $2.8 million, down from $113.2 million the year prior.

Read more:

  • Inside Fifth Third's 'innovation economy' ambitions
  • Citi hires Google's director of engineering, shuffles AI leaders
  • Wells Fargo prevails in pay fight with former CEO Tim Sloan
  • BMO's top US executive to depart in leadership shuffle

Eagle's net interest margin, a measure of how much a bank earns on loans relative to what it pays for deposits and other funding, rose to 2.6% from 2.43% a year earlier. The improvement was driven largely by a shift in its funding mix, as it reduced its reliance on brokered deposits, which lowered funding costs.The bank said lower interest income from declining loan balances partially offset the improvement.

According to Eagle's forward guidance, it expects NIM to be in the range of 2.77% to 3.05% in 2027.

Eagle's earnings per share during the third quarter was 79 cents, easily beating the 37-cent consensus of analysis, according to S&P Capital IQ.

The last time Eagle posted exceeded its third-quarter 2026 net income was in the same period in 2023, when its profits totaled $27.4 million. In the last three years, Eagle has reported losses in four out of 12 quarters, including losses totaling more than $130 million in the second and third quarters of 2025.

data.title: Truist axes 'leadership center' as new CEO scrutinizes bank
data.description:
• Key insight: Truist is closing its executive-leadership institute in Greensboro, North Carolina, as new CEO Mike Lyons takes a hard look at the bank's businesses and operations. The institute used controversial practices, encouraging participants to recall childhood traumas in an effort to improve their leadership skills.
  • Forward look: Truist said it plans to put the Greensboro property, which cost more than $80 million to build and expand, up for sale.

Truist Financial plans to close a leadership center in Greensboro, North Carolina, where its employees go for training, further distancing itself from its pre-merger past and redirecting resources elsewhere.

The decision to shutter the Truist Leadership Institute, which drew criticism for using techniques that involved tapping into childhood trauma to improve would-be executives' leadership skills, comes on the heels of Mike Lyons' arrival last month as CEO. The regional bank is in the midst of a detailed strategic review of each of its businesses, operations and processes, Lyons told analysts last week.

If the review shows that existing businesses, operations and processes are not core to the bank's strategy or generating targeted returns or helping customers, they'll be cut, he said.

The Charlotte, North Carolina-based bank has already made some changes, such as exiting certain, non-core lending portfolios and overhauling the leadership of its consumer-banking business.

"It's not just businesses. It's every process, every operation, every committee, every decision we make," Lyons said on the company's earning call last week. "No sacred cows."

Lyons, a former president of PNC Financial Services Group and CEO of Fiserv, was hired in June to succeed former CEO Bill Rogers. By that time, investors had decided that the 2019 merger that created Truist was a disappointment.

Seven years earlier, executives promised that Truist would become "the premier financial institution of the future." But the company subsequently was criticized for not reaching the financial targets that executives expected to meet, and for not figuring out how to unify two different workplace cultures.

Truist employees were told this week about the closure of the leadership institute, according to an article in the Greensboro News & Record. In a statement shared with American Banker, the bank confirmed that the center's operations will be discontinued by the end of the year.

The eight-year-old campus of the Truist Leadership Institute cost more than $80 million to build and later expand, records show.

Classes will run through mid-December, and the property will be put up for sale, according to a Truist spokesperson. The decision is intended to simplify operations and focus on areas "that help Truist grow, better serve clients and succeed over time," the spokesperson said. The bank is "still shaping" its future leadership-development programming, the spokesperson added.

The Truist Leadership Institute is one of the remaining links to the bank's pre-merger history. Prior to North Carolina-based BB&T's 2019 merger with SunTrust Banks in Atlanta, the center was known as the BB&T Leadership Institute. That merger brought together two of the most prominent Southeast banks, which once together rebranded as Truist.

The leadership institute was a longtime source of pride at BB&T, championed by two former CEOs — John Allison, who was CEO from 1989 to 2008, and later Kelly King.

The center had a close connection to the late psychologist Dr. James Farr, who promoted the idea that unresolved issues from childhood could stunt the personal and professional lives of leaders. BB&T had a business relationship with Farr Associates starting in the 1980s.

In 1994, while Allison was CEO, BB&T acquired Farr Associates, a leadership and management consultancy developed by Farr, who died in 2000. Allison had said that his experience in Farr's program turned him into a believer.

King succeeded Allison as BB&T's CEO and later was CEO of Truist until he retired in the fall of 2021. He was also a supporter of the institute, saying that it helped him become more self-aware.

In 2018, the institute opened a new 60,000-square-foot campus in Greensboro that cost $35 million, according to a press release from the bank. The campus included 48 individual guest rooms, a "Treehouse" meeting room, dining areas, fitness facilities and staff offices.

Reflecting King's "purpose-driven" mindset in banking, which was later embraced by Rogers, his successor at Truist, King said in the 2018 release announcing the new campus: "Our mission is to make the world a better place to live, and we believe one of the best ways to improve our communities is through stronger leaders in all facets of society."

Truist later invested more money into the institute, expanding the size of the campus by 86,000 square feet at a cost of $51.5 million, according to a permit filed in 2023 with the city of Greensboro.

Read more:

  • Inside Fifth Third's 'innovation economy' ambitions
  • Citi hires Google's director of engineering, shuffles AI leaders
  • Wells Fargo prevails in pay fight with former CEO Tim Sloan
  • BMO's top US executive to depart in leadership shuffle

Truist did not say how many people the institute employs. The center's LinkedIn page — which describes programming as a "one-of-a-kind, science-based leadership development experience designed with a deep understanding of human nature" — says the "company size" is 51 to 200 people. The center offers programming to individuals outside of Truist in addition to the bank's employees.

The Truist spokesperson said the company is "committed to supporting" the center's employees, including finding them other jobs at Truist and providing severance benefits and job-search assistance.

data.title: New law requires dating apps to help block romance scams
data.description:
• Key insight: The new law mostly codifies existing practice. Most dating services already send fraud-ban notices to all users because at least four states require them, and the federal law overrides those state rules.
  • Supporting data: Among victims who told the FTC how they paid, bank transfers carried the most romance-scam losses in 2025, at $195 million, ahead of cryptocurrency at $159 million.

Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review.

A newly signed law saddles dating apps with a federal duty to help stop romance scams: They must warn users when someone who messaged them gets banned for fraud. Most dating apps already issue such warnings.

President Trump on Tuesday signed the Romance Scam Prevention Act, which requires online dating services to notify any user who received a message from an account the service later banned for fraud. The law takes effect October 2027.

The warning is designed to help users who have moved their conversation with the scammer off the dating app, onto another messaging platform. The notice must tell users not to send money or financial information to anyone else on the app.

For banks, the law starts to shift some accountability for romance scams to dating apps, something banking trade groups have been asking for. It's is also a small first answer to a question consumer advocates have been pressing in Washington: Who should bear responsibility when a scam starts on a tech platform?

There is "no clear or consistent duty of care to suppress scam activity" across telecom companies, digital platforms and financial services, according to a national strategy an Aspen Institute task force released last year.

The task force's members included banks, the American Bankers Association and the Bank Policy Institute.

The new law creates one such duty, for one kind of platform. That duty is a notice, not reimbursement.

What the dating-app notice says, and who already sends it

The notice must identify the banned profile and say that the person "may have been using a false identity or attempting to defraud members," according to the text of the law. It must also include advice on avoiding fraud.

The law puts no limit on how long ago the message arrived. The notice generally must go out within 24 hours of the ban and must say when the user last traded messages with the banned account.

The only people whose privacy the law affects are those banned for fraud, according to the Senate Commerce Committee's report on the bill.

The Federal Trade Commission, or FTC, and state attorneys general enforce the law. Services that comply get a safe harbor, meaning no user, including the banned one, can sue the service over sending a required notice.

The law also sets "one national standard," according to its text, overriding state laws on the same subject.

At least four states require dating apps to provide notification of sketchy users: Vermont since 2017, Arizona since 2021, Utah since 2024 and New York since 2025.

The pre-existence of the state laws means the federal mandate changes little in practice. Most dating services already send the notices to users nationwide "because some states already require those fraud notifications," according to the Congressional Budget Office's cost estimate for the Senate version of the bill.

The federal notice closely tracks those state rules but reaches more people. The state laws require notices only for users who replied to the banned account; the federal law covers anyone who received a message from a banned account.

Where romance scams start, and where the law stops

Consumers reported losing $1.48 billion to romance scams in 2025, up 22% from the year before, according to the FTC.

Victims who told the FTC how they paid lost more through bank transfers ($195 million) than through any other method, ahead of cryptocurrency ($159 million), according to the agency's public fraud-data dashboard. (Most reports did not name a payment method.)

Many of those scams never touch a dating app. Nearly 60% of people who reported losing money to a romance scam in 2025 said the deception started on social media, according to an April FTC data analysis.

The law signed Tuesday covers dating services specifically, not social media in general.

On dating apps, the notice goes out only after the app decides to ban an account, but these apps do not always catch scammers quickly.

As of the second half of 2025, Tinder had gone years without updating most of the machine-learning models it uses to catch scammers, according to an Oct. 13 report from Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., the top Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee.

In the first nine months of 2025, nearly 500,000 scammers or other bad actors on Tinder and Hinge in the U.S. swapped contact information with another user, the report found.

The newly required notices target the transition off the dating app, onto a messaging platform.

The app doesn't need to know whether that transition actually happened; the notice goes out by email or text message, so it reaches a user who took the conversation elsewhere and would not otherwise learn the dating app banned the account.

Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, rolled out new detection models and a video-selfie check for new Tinder users after the investigation began, according to the report.

Match Group supports the law and welcomes "a national standard that builds on the protections our apps already provide," a company spokesperson told American Banker in a statement.

"Romance scams are a societal problem that spans every online platform, and no company can solve alone," the spokesperson said.

Why a dating-app rule matters to banks

Romance-scam victims usually don't recover their losses. When a scammer tricks a customer into authorizing a payment, the bank generally does not have to refund it under Regulation E, the federal rule on disputed electronic transfers.

That line is under pressure. The United Kingdom began requiring sending and receiving banks to split the cost of reimbursing scam victims in October 2024, under rules from its Payment Systems Regulator.

House Democrats have proposed a similar split in the U.S. in the Protecting Consumers from Payment Scams Act. House Financial Services Committee Republicans rejected that approach in a July report on fraud policy.

The dating-app law takes another route by putting a duty on a platform rather than on the bank, although that duty does not require any kind of reimbursement for losses.

The Independent Community Bankers of America called the law "an ICBA-supported bill" in a Sept. 29 post after the Senate passed it.

The new law cuts both ways for banks. On one hand, it gives dating apps cover: An app that sends notices as the law requires has done what Congress asked of it, leaving banks that move the money looking more responsible when a scam succeeds anyway.

But if the notices prevent potential victims from sending money, there are fewer losses for anyone to fight over.

data.title: Gould: banks preparing for rogue AI agents for 'months'
data.description:
• Key insight: Major banks are using their own artificial intelligence software to protect depositors against reported breaches stemming from an internet-wide code vulnerability.
  • Expert quote: "The banks have been all over this for months now, fortifying their defenses and using SI as a defense against these AI agents, too." — Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould.

NEW YORK — The comptroller of the currency said banks are well-positioned to guard against cyber attacks and data breaches from artificial intelligence programs.

In a television interview Thursday morning, Comptroller Jonathan Gould attempted to ease depositor concerns after reports surfaced this week that unauthorized AI agents have gained access to a wide swatch of websites and online platforms — including those that connect bank customers with their accounts.

In his appearance on Fox Business's "Varney & Co." program, Gould said many banks are using their own AI systems — which he referred to as SI, for super intelligence — to block bad actors from moving funds.

"The banks have been all over this for months now, fortifying their defenses and using SI as a defense against these AI agents, too," Gould said, noting that he recently toured the operation of a major national bank to see the technology work up close. "I'm here to assure you that SI is a powerful defensive weapon as well."

Stuart Varney, the host of the program, asked Gould twice whether customers could expect to get their funds back, should an unauthorized AI agent transfer money out. Gould did not specify how such matters would be resolved. Instead, he reiterated his confidence in the ability for banks to block such activities in the first place.

Read more:

  • As fintechs nab bank charters, what's happening to BaaS?
  • Overheated data center knocked 23 credit unions offline
  • Chris Britt still says banking is broken, but Chime can fix it
  • Credit unions bulk up a business that banks long dominated

"Well, again, banks are very focused on defending the frontier," he said. "Banks are some of the most fortified parts of our system, and we have been across the U.S. government very focused on making sure that they have the latest tools so they can defend themselves — not just the banks, but also the service providers that are part of that system as well."

Gould's TV appearance came one day after the disclosure of critical weaknesses in core PHP, a popular coding language that is used by roughly 70% of websites on the internet. The vulnerabilities, referred to as PHP2Shell, were discovered by a pair of AI research groups, Wiz Research and Calif, in August.

A patch for the vulnerabilities was implemented on Wednesday, but it appears some bad actors may have already exploited the weaknesses. On Thursday morning, Axios reported that unauthorized third-party AI agents breached customer accounts at several large U.S. banks, including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorganChase, Wells Fargo and other banks. Axios attributed the report to unnamed sources.

Gould did not refute the claims that banks had been breached.

Removing the debanking 'temptation'

During his brief appearance, Gould said his agency — which supervises banks with national charters — was taking steps to fortify the banking industry against what he sees as another key threat: debanking.

Gould said the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency is working with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and other agencies to implement regulatory changes that would discourage banks from closing customer accounts for political reasons.

"We're very focused on making sure that we make changes at the OCC and the regulatory framework to reduce the temptation that banks will have in the future to allow themselves to be used for these types of debanking actions going forward," Gould said. "So, we want to make sure that we're doing everything we can, just as we're fortifying the system against SI attacks, we're also fortifying the system from the attacks of either internal activists at banks or external activists too."

Gould did not specify what regulatory change would be made to achieve this goal. His comments after his agency released a comprehensive report on debanking last week.

data.title: As smaller rivals keep quiet, Axos opens up on custody fees
data.description:
When it comes to RIA custody, silence is part of the structure, industry experts said. That seemed to be borne out in this latest installment of Financial Planning's series on industry custodians, which focuses on three smaller players: Hilltop Securities and Innovayte, which declined any form of interview about their fees and business models, and Axos Advisor Services, which initially declined but reversed course this week.

That apparent reluctance, however, does not reveal "anything firm-specific," according to William Trout, director of the securities and investments practice at consulting firm Datos Insights, and Gregory O'Gara, a strategic advisor with Datos' wealth management practice. Instead, they argued in an email that it reflects custodians' general dependence on cash sweeps, which also came up in a "risk alert" issued by the Securities and Exchange Commission in June.   

"Reticence here is structural by nature: Silence is the default posture in this segment of the business. Pricing is negotiated firm by firm, and cash sweep arrangements are under regulatory scrutiny," Trout and O'Gara said. "SEC examiners flagged advisers that failed to disclose revenue they receive from 'some custodians' based on client cash balances. For example, a clearing firm or custodian sweeps uninvested client cash into money market funds or bank deposit products. It then pays the adviser, or the adviser's affiliated broker-dealer, a share of the resulting revenue based on how much cash the adviser's clients hold. Where these arrangements exist, the custodian is the paying party, and custody executives rarely discuss pricing or cash sweep revenue on the record."

The 3 firms, at a glance

Las Vegas-based Axos, Dallas-based Hilltop and Dallas-based Innovayte may not be the first firms that come to mind for registered investment advisory firm owners and financial advisors when thinking about the industry's custodians. But they each operate substantial clearing and custody businesses. 

Axos' serves hundreds of RIAs and other wealth management firms. Hilltop's publicly traded parent company reported more than 90 clients for its custody and other services. And after ending its outsourced vendor relationship with Axos to start its own custody business in 2023, Innovayte reported $3.4 billion in assets, largely in alternative investments, through predecessor firms that provided custody for self-directed individual retirement accounts. 

When Innovayte broke into the business, CEO Catherine "Cat" Davies said the firm aimed to work with RIAs that had between $100 million and $800 million in assets under management. Earlier this month, Davies' team appointed former Apex Fintech Solutions Chief Operating Officer Fritz Louis-Charles to be Innovayte's COO.

"Innovayte has built a strong foundation, and I look forward to working alongside this talented team to scale our operations, strengthen our risk and controls environment and continue delivering an exceptional experience for our clients," Louis-Charles said in a statement.

The other Dallas-based custodian, Hilltop, is part of the broker-dealer segment of Hilltop Holdings, a banking, mortgage, municipal investment, insurance and asset management company that also owns a midsize broker-dealer. In the second quarter, the unit housing Hilltop's clearing and custody business generated pretax profit of $12.4 million on net revenue of $124 million for a margin of 10%.

At the end of last year, Hilltop's custodian provided "trade execution and clearance as well as back office services such as recordkeeping, trade reporting, accounting, general back-office support, securities and margin lending, reorganization assistance and custody of securities" to "93 financial organizations, including correspondent firms, correspondent broker-dealers, registered investment advisers, discount and full-service brokerage firms and institutional firms," according to its parent firm's last annual report.

Axos' custody strategy and fees

Axos Financial, a publicly traded bank and digital wealth management firm, has expanded its custody line to a larger size than the other two firms. It bought the business — previously known as Trust Company of America and E-Trade Advisor Services — from Morgan Stanley in 2021 for $55 million. 

In the end, Axos was more willing to talk about its fees and business models than not only the silent Hilltop and Innovayte, but also two giants of the industry, Fidelity Investments and BNY Pershing, whose representatives answered questions via email but didn't agree to live interviews. 

Axos also shared its standard fee schedule. 

Mike Watson, executive vice president and head of Axos Clearing and Advisor Services, compared the schedule to the "rack rate" or the costs displayed on the back of the door in a hotel room. RIAs and other wealth management clients negotiate asset-based fees or transaction prices, with the talks beginning "with understanding what they're paying today, what's important to them," and an evaluation of how working together could benefit both parties, Watson said.

"It really depends on the firm and how they want to utilize us as a custodian," Watson said. "A lot of it has to do with what they're paying where they're at." 

He added that Axos is having "lots of conversations with prospects," particularly in the wake of Fidelity's looming move to drop RIAs with less than $100 million on its custody platform. 

Axos' figures show its custody business has grown since leaving Morgan Stanley. When the business changed hands five years ago, Axos listed $23 billion in assets under custody or administration across 200 client RIAs, advisory practices and other wealth management firms. As of the end of the second quarter this year, the firm had $47.8 billion and 300 clearing and custody clients. Compared to the second quarter of 2020, the clearing and custody firm's net revenue has soared by more than 350% to $41.4 million, according to Axos' investor presentation from August. The "secular" trends in the industry including fee compression, advisor independence, succession planning challenges and the onslaught of digital technology "provide opportunities for Axos," the presentation said.

The firm's ideal clients fit into one or more of "three buckets," according to Watson. The first revolves around firms that have "an orientation toward planning" that could go "deeper" with banking and other Axos capabilities. The second stems from firms with mass affluent to "single-digit millionaire" customers, and the third is among RIAs with less than $500 million in AUM, he said.

"That segment feels underserved and underappreciated," Watson said. "So we think we have an opportunity." 

Nevertheless, the firm also faces some of the same compliance challenges as many companies operating in wealth management. 

Earlier this year, a FINRA arbitration panel ordered Axos Clearing to pay $49.4 million in damages and attorney fees to the former clients of a defunct brokerage that used its clearing and back-office services. Axos is seeking to vacate the decision in federal court. The judge hasn't ruled yet on its motion to toss the arbitration decision or the filing by the clients seeking confirmation of the award. 

Custodians often face litigation from former clients of brokerage or other wealth management firms who say they were harmed by fraud or faulty recommendations using the clearing and custody firms' infrastructure. At Axos, the expenses from the case helped cut pretax profits in half for the last fiscal year for the segment of its business that includes the clearing and custody firm.

data.title: BankThink A 'double-flywheel' effect is about to transform financial services
data.description:
• Key insight: The application of AI agents operating on new payment rails and the rapid adoption of tokenized assets will work together to drive changes to the banking industry at an unprecedented pace, scale and breadth.
  • Expert quote: "We overestimate the impact of technology in the short-term and underestimate the effect in the long run." —Roy Amara

This is the second article in a three-part series. The first piece explored how the combination of digital assets and AI agents are going to rapidly transform the banking industry.

In more than two decades of working in payments and transaction banking, I have not experienced change as profound and as rapid as what we are facing now. The pace, scale and velocity of innovation that the industry is experiencing are unmatched. I see two reasons for this.

The first one is the combination of AI and digital assets that is creating a perfect storm of conditions for ever-increasing levels of automation, efficiency, effectiveness, and speed. Agentic AI will serve as an accelerant as the economic actors of the future are not likely to be human, but rather bots. AI agents will require rails that are fit for purpose: rails that are programmable, always-on, and frictionless. These automated agents will increasingly and systematically drive financial transaction traffic toward the rails that are the most efficient and effective; and as a result, drive adoption without requiring humans to adapt their behavior. In innovations of the past, the main limiting factor in the adoption of new technology has been the relatively slow pace at which humans adapt their behaviors. The rapid cycles of tech innovation usually outpace human capacity to change. But I often wonder to myself, "What if humans are not the ones making the decision on which product best meets their financial needs?" AI will seek solutions that are better, faster, available, cost effective and seamless.

In addition to AI, there is another force driving more rapid adoption of tokenization, and that is a flywheel effect between payments and capital markets. It is not just about tokenization of money or tokenization of other assets as siloed and stand-alone innovations. The tokenization of both money and real-world assets, or RWAs, are mutually reinforcing and will put pressure on both sides to evolve and keep up. The promise and benefits of tokenized money and tokenized RWAs are not complete without each other, and this will create mutual pressure for faster development and adoption of tokenization across the full value chain in financial services.

While the two forces above are distinct, they will have compounding effects and drive greater levels of innovation and adoption. This double flywheel effect is why I believe the level and pace of change is unmatched.

In addition to the speed of change, I often think about the scale and breadth of the change. I often hear questions on the value of tokenization, and hear versions of the statement that digital assets "are a solution in search of a problem." Or that "clients are not asking for this."

My first reaction to those statements is that many financial processes are inefficient, error-prone, expensive and filled with friction; and one does not need to go in search of problems. There are plenty of client problems waiting to be solved, and many problems that we have been unable to solve with legacy technology. We do not need to do much searching to find opportunities to deliver better solutions. And while clients may not explicitly ask for tokenized solutions, they seek simple, efficient and integrated ways to manage money and assets. Product leaders should anticipate and address client pain points, rather than wait for the client to define and ask for a better solution. If a client asks for a specific solution, it is because a competitor has already educated them on the potential of the solution; and as a result, the competitor has already set the standards and expectations. I would much prefer being the one to define the vision of what is possible in the eyes of a client.

My second reaction to those statements is that we may have caused our own problems when we talk about the promise of technology. Are we so enamored with technology for the sake of itself that we forget the problems it is meant to solve — or to explain it and make it tangible? In some ways, our own hype is crowding out real problem solving and damaging our ability to move innovation forward. This level of hype can lead to a loss of credibility. As with any product innovation, we need to keep ourselves grounded and intellectually honest. And that means answering three key questions: What is the client problem that we are trying to solve? Why is this a problem worth solving? and How do we solve it (and why do we have the right to be the ones to solve it)?

If we answer those questions, then the story about digital assets becomes far more compelling.

Another frequent topic of discussion is whether digital assets are a product or a rail. And my answer is that they are both — and they are neither.

Read more:

  • 'We could lose our edge': Bankers on competing for digital assets
  • How Barclays plans to grow its U.S.-based digital bank
  • M&T says it's monitoring impact of AI agents on deposits
  • Why Chase is rethinking workflows as AI adoption accelerates

"Both" because tokenized forms of money and RWAs enable new features and capabilities for clients (improved product), and also because they enable faster, easier and cheaper movement of value and assets (better rails).

"Neither" because framing it in this way is far too narrow and limits us in our ability to imagine a future that is vastly different from what we have now.

The analogy I think of is mobile phones. One could have argued 25 years ago that cell phones are a better product (a smaller, more compact, more accessible phone) and a better "rail" (we could make voice calls without being tethered to a wall). But describing cell phones as simply a better product or rail for making voice calls underestimates how they have evolved and the impact they now have on our daily lives and activities.

The problem with a product or rail view of innovation is that we are limited by the uses we are familiar with at that moment in time; e.g., our thinking 25 years ago that mobile phones were a better product and rail for making voice calls. I imagine that for most of us today, the use of cell phones for voice calls represents less than 10% to 15% of the total usage. And yet, how many of us could have imagined 25 years ago all of the apps, functions, capabilities and enablers that fill the other 85% to 90% of our usage? How many activities do we perform on our phones that have nothing to do with phone calls? How many industries, new offerings, and new business and revenue models have proliferated as a result of mobile phone technology?

This is called Amara's law. Roy Amara was a computer scientist who said, "We overestimate the impact of technology in the short-term and underestimate the effect in the long run." We get tied up in the short-term functionality and benefits, and lack the ability to comprehend the compounding effect: Each innovation leads to further innovation that would not have been possible without the previous one. It is relatively easy to understand immediate and visible benefits of new technology, but nearly impossible to imagine what it will be in the future after multiple compounded innovation hops. A physics professor Albert Allen Bartlett put it best when he said: "The greatest shortcoming of the human race is man's inability to understand the exponential function."

My guess is that the exponential effects of tokenization of money and assets are likely to lead us down a path we are not yet capable of envisioning. A future where new businesses, business models and revenue pools we cannot yet anticipate will exist, perhaps overtaking many of the products and solutions that exist in financial services today — similar to how other uses and products, made possible by mobile phones, have surpassed usage related to voice calls.

data.title: Stablecoins need more than yield; they need ubiquity
data.description:
Let's say you are a company in the money business. People give you money, and you give them tools that help them do things with that money. To entice people into keeping their money with you rather than some competitor, you also offer them a small monetary reward at a predetermined rate paid out on a predetermined schedule. You call this payment interest, or yield.

If your business is called a bank and observes a set of very specific rules, this arrangement is standard. If your business is not called a bank, this arrangement is not at all standard. This arrangement in fact can be rather illegal. Unless, that is, you don't call it interest, or yield. 

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency on Wednesday finalized its version of the new rules for stablecoins, as our Ebrima Santos Sanneh reported, that left the door slightly ajar for stablecoin issuers to offer what are essentially interest payments on customer accounts. 

The OCC's final rule does ban direct interest payments from issuers to customers. But the OCC also said it would look at rewards arrangements on an individual basis. As our story notes, the OCC acknowledged that some "arrangements" would fall afoul of the yield ban, but others might not. In other words, it might be possible for a stablecoin issuer to rig up their business in such a way that they are in effect paying customers some amount of money to entice the customer to keep their money with the issuer.

What that ends up meaning, in practice, is that all these stablecoins issuers are almost certainly going to start figuring out how they can rig a yield-paying mechanism into their businesses that isn't a straight-up interest payment. It will effectively be interest; they just won't call that. Knowing cryptopians, they'll invent some nonsense word for it that nobody understands. 

The banking industry has been adamantly against giving this option to stablecoin companies, the fearing being that those companies will become competitors. It's a possibility.

But the problem that the stablecoin companies have not so far gotten around is that the only people interested in their product are people in the crypto financial system, for the simple reason that that is the only place where stablecoins are used or accepted. 

Read more:

  • Forget jobs or inflation, credit is what matters. And credit is…
  • For both de novos and prediction markets, it's how you read the law
  • Those sleepy deposits that are 90% of your customers are waking up
  • Crypto and bitcoin have problems the CFTC and SEC can't fix

And the crypto market is a weird, mostly stagnant place. A handful of cryptos dominate it and it's never really made any inroads into the mainstream. Not only are the dominant cryptos — bitcoin, ether, tether, circle — not accepted universally outside of crypto markets, they are not accepted even marginally. I could walk the length of Broadway and probably would not find five stores that accepted any of them. Maybe not three. 

I have stated this before, but it bears repeating: what makes a currency useful is ubiquity. It has to be accepted everywhere by everyone. The easiest way to achieve this, of course, is via the law. The U.S. dollar is universally accepted by law. Crypto companies have a hard time competing with that. Which is why the fight over yield, in terms of who is on offense and who is on defense, is actually backwards. The crypto companies need to be able to offer yield-like products far more desperately than the banks need to block those products.
